book.title: Yes! 50 Scientifically Proven Ways to Be Persuasive
book.author: Noah J. Goldstein, Steve J. Martin and Robert B. Cialdini

confidence_note: Chapter 14's title and its in-home survey example come from a library table of contents and a chapter summary; the Freedman and Fraser figures come from Wikipedia's account of the 1966 paper. The old text's sign study is the same paper's second study and is attributed to the paper, not to the book. Effect sizes in later work are smaller and mixed.
facts: Chapter 14: 'How can one small step help your influence take a giant leap?'; agreement to a small request roughly doubles agreement to a much larger one.
Freedman and Fraser 1966: California housewives were phoned and asked to answer a few questions about household products they used.

Three days later: could five or six men come into the home for two hours and go through cupboards and storage places? 52.8 percent of those who had answered the questions agreed; those asked only the large request were less than half as likely to agree.
Same paper: small window sign then large 'Drive Carefully' lawn sign, 76 percent against 17 percent.
Later work is mixed: donation studies sometimes found no significant effect.
scene_details: A phone call about household products.
Five or six men, two hours, cupboards and storage places.
A small window sign and a large lawn sign.
tension: A request for two hours of strangers in the house got a much better answer after a few phone questions.
opening_idea: Start with the second phone call and its size.

lessons.idea: Begin with a small request that the person can say yes to.
lessons.anchor: The questions on the phone before the two-hour request.

reflect_final: What small first step could you ask of someone before you ask for the larger thing you really want?

use_cases.move: The household survey began with a few questions; I'll ask for one small task before the bigger role.

use_cases.situation: Asking a neighbour for a shared project
use_cases.move: Ask for a small thing first, with a real reason, and let them decide.

use_cases.situation: Starting a habit with a partner
use_cases.move: Agree on one small step together before planning the whole routine.

pocket_idea: A few phone questions made two hours of strangers in the house far more likely a yes.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Women who first answered a few questions were twice as likely to let strangers in for two hours.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: The phone calls and the 52.8 percent.
